newsitem.title: FINLAND: PK CABLES CEO SEES TELECOMS SALES GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: PK CABLES CEO SEES TELECOMS SALES GROWTH.

text.p: Finnish industrial wiring group PK Cables Oy expects net sales in its telecoms related business growing 25-30 percent in 1997, the group's chief executive said on Friday.
Newly listed PK Cables is aiming for group net sales growth to 500 million markka within three to five years, from 260 million in 1996, CEO Tom Hakalax told Reuters in an interview.
"Net sales growth of about 25-30 percent in our telecoms equipment business this year would be normal and manageable," he said.
Deliveries to the telecommunications industry had risen from nil to become the group's fastest growing sector in just over half a year.

Some 45 million markka, or 59 percent of 1996 net sales growth, came from the assembly of mobile phone network base station frameworks under subcontract to Finnish telecoms group Nokia Oy . Assembly began in August last year.

"We don't need to dream about growth," Hakalax said, referring specifically to the telecoms related business. "It's more a question whether the growth can be controlled and, if necessary, even slowed down."
He added there were "no big problems controlling growth."
Asked how this year was shaping up, Hakalax said: "As planned -- both in terms of profitability and net sales."
He declined to give profit targets for this year, but said the medium-term goal, over a period of three to five years, was to keep operating profit above 10 percent of turnover.
Another medium-term goal is to raise annual net sales to over 500 million markka, he said. The horizon for that target was three to five years, but "probably closer to three."

"Growth itself is not the main goal...For us it is more important to fulfil our earnings objectives." said Hakalax, who owns over six percent of the company after selling part of his stake in an initial public offering in March.
In 1996, PK Cable's net sales grew 41.5 percent, to 260 million markka from 184 million in 1995. Profit after financial items was 37 million markka, up from 29 million in 1995.
In the future, the group plans to pay out "at least a third" of its profits in dividend, Hakalax said. The dividend for 1996, 1.00 markka per share, was about 20 percent of EPS at 5.11 markka.
PK Cables' main business is wiring systems for the heavy vehicle industry. In 1996, group sales of wiring systems for the truck industry accounted for over 70 percent of total net sales.
"Net sales in our truck wiring business will grow over 20 percent this year," Hakalax said.

Despite the fast growth in the telecommunications equipment sector, the company reaps "significantly bigger" margins making cable harnesses -- the cabling that makes up a truck's electrical systems -- Hakalax said, but declined to give margin figures.
Prices in the subcontracting business tended to decline over time, and the constant challenge was to raise efficiency "because you can't always take it out of margins", he said.
Much of the company's competitiveness in the work-intensive vehicle wiring business was due to extensive use of subcontracted labour in low-cost Estonia and Russia, he added.

Almost 70 percent of the company's total manual labour input is purchased from subcontractors -- mainly Estonian Harju Elekter AS, which is also PK Cables' single biggest owner with a 10 percent stake, Hakalax said.
PK Cables will report first-quarter earnings on April 28 at 1000/0700 GMT, and would then also give an outlook for 1997, Hakalax said.
